[RELEASED] Abraxas (HES2011)
This wargame was introduced at the Hackito Ergo Sum (HES) 2011 conference in Paris and is centered around the fictitious company dildosfromspace.com
The wargame has its own website with the entire backstory. You can find it here.
As of September 2011, the Abraxas game has been released to the public and can be downloaded here.
The following instructions are also included on the diskimage:
Study guide
This guide explains what Abraxas is and how to run it safely. It does not describe the challenges, which are meant to be discovered.
What it is

Abraxas was introduced at the Hackito Ergo Sum (HES) conference in Paris in 2011. It is centred on a fictitious company, and the game has its own website containing the whole backstory. Since September 2011 it has been released to the public and can be downloaded as an .ova virtual-machine image from the OverTheWire image server.
How it differs from the SSH games

Games such as Bandit and Narnia run on OverTheWire servers. Abraxas runs on your own computer: you import the virtual machine and play entirely offline. Instructions for the game are included on the disk image itself, which is why the upstream page ends with a heading and nothing below it.
Getting started
Download the OVA file from the link on the page (it is a large file; verify the download completes).
Import it into VirtualBox or another hypervisor that supports OVA.
Read the instructions on the image and the backstory website, then start investigating.
Run it safely
Isolate the network. These images are intentionally vulnerable. Use a host-only or internal network in your hypervisor so the machine is not reachable from the internet or your home network.
Snapshot before you start. A snapshot lets you roll back after you break something.
Use a disposable environment. A spare virtual machine host, not the laptop that holds your real data.
Change default credentials if you ever connect a lab image to a shared network.
Keep notes. Story-driven games reward writing down every credential, host and clue as you find it.
Where this fits
Conference wargames suit people who have already completed several of the main games, such as Bandit, Natas and Narnia, and want story-driven, multi-step challenges.

Level Goal

The goal of this level is for you to log into the game using SSH. The host to which you need to connect is bandit.labs.overthewire.org, on port 2220. The username is bandit0 and the password is bandit0. Once logged in, go to the Level 1 page to find out how to beat Level 1.
Commands you may need to solve this level
ssh
Helpful Reading Material
Secure Shell (SSH) on Wikipedia
How to use SSH with a non-standard port on It’s FOSS
How to use SSH with ssh-keys on wikiHow
Study guide
Level map: this is the starting line. You log in as bandit0 (password bandit0); logging in successfully is the whole level.
What this level teaches

How to open a secure remote shell. Almost everything in OverTheWire, and most real-world server administration, starts with SSH (Secure Shell): a client on your machine opens an encrypted connection to an SSH server and gives you a command line on the remote computer.
Key ideas
Host — the machine you connect to, here bandit.labs.overthewire.org.
Port — a numbered door on that machine. SSH normally listens on 22, but this server uses 2220, so you must pass the port explicitly. Every OverTheWire game has its own port.
Credentials — a username and password prove who you are. The terminal deliberately shows nothing while you type a password; that is normal, not a frozen screen.

Host key fingerprint — the first time you connect, SSH asks whether to trust the server and remembers its fingerprint in ~/.ssh/known_hosts. If the fingerprint ever changes, SSH warns you that someone may be impersonating the server.
How to approach it
Open a terminal. macOS and Linux include ssh; recent Windows versions include it in Command Prompt and PowerShell, and PuTTY is a graphical alternative.
The command has the shape ssh USER@HOST -p PORT. Fill the three values in from the Level Goal and read the -p option in man ssh if you are unsure.
After logging in, run whoami and pwd to confirm who and where you are, then exit to disconnect. You will repeat this login dance for every level.
Why it matters
SSH is how engineers administer servers, deploy code and tunnel traffic. Understanding hosts, ports and host-key verification is the foundation for everything that follows.

Level Goal

The password for the next level is stored in a file called readme located in the home directory. Use this password to log into bandit1 using SSH. Whenever you find a password for a level, use SSH (on port 2220) to log into that level and continue the game.
Commands you may need to solve this level
ls , cd , cat , file , du , find
TIP: Create a file for notes and passwords on your local machine!
Passwords for levels are not saved automatically. If you do not save them yourself, you will need to start over from bandit0.

Passwords also occasionally change. It is recommended to take notes on how to solve each challenge. As levels get more challenging, detailed notes are useful to return to where you left off, reference for later problems, or help others after you’ve completed the challenge.
Study guide
Level map: logged in as bandit0, find the password for bandit1.
What this level teaches
Orientation in a Unix filesystem and your first real data-gathering commands. A password is waiting in an ordinary file; the skill is knowing where you are and how to look inside a file.
Key ideas
Home directory — the folder you land in after logging in, shorthand ~. pwd prints the current directory.
ls lists a directory’s contents. Options such as -l (long format) and -a (include hidden entries) change what you see.
cat prints a file’s contents to the terminal.
Everything is a file — on Unix, configuration, devices and passwords are all just files with permissions.
How to approach it
Look around before acting: pwd, then ls.
Print the file that the Level Goal names.
Copy the result into your notes file. The password is plain text, and the next level’s login (ssh bandit1@...) needs it.
Why it matters
“Where am I, what is here, what does it say?” is the loop you will run thousands of times, on every system you ever investigate.

Level Goal
The password for the next level is stored in the file data.txt in one of the few human-readable strings, preceded by several ‘=’ characters.
Commands you may need to solve this level
grep, sort, uniq, strings, base64, tr, tar, gzip, bzip2, xxd
Study guide
Level map: logged in as bandit9, find the password for bandit10.
What this level teaches
Finding human-readable fragments inside data that is mostly binary.
Key ideas
strings scans a file and prints runs of printable characters. It is a first-look tool for reverse engineers and malware analysts.
Binary vs text. Most of the file is non-printable bytes; the interesting part is a handful of text fragments.
Combining tools. strings produces many lines, and grep narrows them to those matching the clue (several = characters).
How to approach it
Try cat on the file and note how unhelpful it is (use reset afterwards if your terminal is garbled).
Pipe strings into grep using the pattern described in the Level Goal.
Why it matters
strings is often the very first command run on an unknown executable. You will use it again in Leviathan and other binary games.

Level Goal
The password for the next level is stored in the file data.txt, which contains base64 encoded data
Commands you may need to solve this level
grep, sort, uniq, strings, base64, tr, tar, gzip, bzip2, xxd
Helpful Reading Material
Base64 on Wikipedia
Study guide
Level map: logged in as bandit10, find the password for bandit11.
What this level teaches
What Base64 is, how to recognise it, and how to reverse it.
Key ideas
Encoding vs encryption. Base64 represents arbitrary bytes using 64 safe text characters so they survive email, URLs and JSON. It involves no key and provides no secrecy.
Recognising Base64. Letters, digits, + and /, often with = padding at the end, in lines of regular length.
base64 -d decodes; run without -d it encodes.
How to approach it
Look at the file and note the telltale alphabet.
Decode it with the base64 command; check the manual for the decode flag.
Try encoding a short phrase and decoding it back to see the round trip.
Why it matters
Base64 appears in HTTP headers, tokens, certificates and email. Mistaking it for encryption is a common real-world security error.

text: Source: This content is aggregated from overthewire (MIT). Visit the original repository for the latest version.
Level Goal
The password for the next level is stored in the file data.txt, where all lowercase (a-z) and uppercase (A-Z) letters have been rotated by 13 positions
Commands you may need to solve this level
grep, sort, uniq, strings, base64, tr, tar, gzip, bzip2, xxd
Helpful Reading Material
Rot13 on Wikipedia
Study guide
Level map: logged in as bandit11, find the password for bandit12.
What this level teaches
Substitution ciphers, and character translation with tr.
Key ideas

ROT13 replaces each letter by the one 13 places later in the alphabet, wrapping around. Because the alphabet has 26 letters, applying ROT13 twice returns the original, so the same operation encrypts and decrypts.
tr SET1 SET2 replaces each character of the first set with the corresponding character of the second. Ranges such as a-e are allowed, so tr 'a-e' 'A-E' upper-cases only those five letters.
ROT13 is trivially reversible and provides obfuscation, not security.
How to approach it
Work out by hand where A and a land after a 13-place shift, and write the two sets so every letter is covered.
Remember upper and lower case need their own ranges.
Test your tr command on a word you encode yourself before applying it to the real file.
Why it matters
This is the first step of Krypton, where simple ciphers like this are attacked systematically with frequency analysis.

text: Source: This content is aggregated from overthewire (MIT). Visit the original repository for the latest version.
Level Goal

The password for the next level is stored in the file data.txt, which is a hexdump of a file that has been repeatedly compressed. For this level it may be useful to create a directory under /tmp in which you can work. Use mkdir with a hard to guess directory name. Or better, use the command “mktemp -d”. Then copy the datafile using cp, and rename it using mv (read the manpages!)
Commands you may need to solve this level
grep, sort, uniq, strings, base64, tr, tar, gzip, bzip2, xxd, mkdir, cp, mv, file
Helpful Reading Material
Hex dump on Wikipedia
Study guide
Level map: logged in as bandit12, find the password for bandit13.
What this level teaches
A repeatable loop for dealing with unknown, nested data: identify, unpack, repeat.
Key ideas
Hexdump. xxd shows bytes as hexadecimal; xxd -r reverses a dump back into the original binary.
Compression formats. gzip, bzip2 and tar archives each begin with a recognisable signature, so file can name them at every layer.
Extension expectations. gzip -d and bzip2 -d expect matching filename suffixes, so you will rename files with mv between steps.

A private working directory. You cannot normally create files in your home directory. Make a new one under /tmp with mktemp -d, which picks a name nobody can guess, and copy the data file into it with cp.
How to approach it
Reverse the hexdump into a file.
Run file on it, apply the matching tool, and run file on the result. Repeat until you see plain text.
Keep notes of the chain you followed; it is easy to lose your place.
Why it matters
Malware droppers, CTF challenges and forensic images are frequently layered. A calm identify-and-unpack loop beats guessing.

text: Source: This content is aggregated from overthewire (MIT). Visit the original repository for the latest version.
Level Goal

The password for the next level is stored in /etc/bandit_pass/bandit14 and can only be read by user bandit14. For this level, you don’t get the next password, but you get a private SSH key that can be used to log into the next level. Look at the commands that logged you into previous bandit levels, and find out how to use the key for this level.
Commands you may need to solve this level
ssh, scp, umask, chmod, cat, nc, install
Helpful Reading Material
SSH/OpenSSH/Keys
Study guide
Level map: logged in as bandit13, gain access to bandit14.
What this level teaches
Public-key authentication, the way professionals actually log in to servers.
Key ideas
Key pairs. A private key stays secret with you; the matching public key sits on the server. The server proves you hold the private key without the key ever crossing the network.
Strict permissions. ssh refuses to use a private key that other users can read, printing “UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE”. Keys need mode 600.
ssh -i FILE names the identity (private key) to use.
Copying files. scp copies files over SSH, and the same server can also connect back to itself.
How to approach it
Find the key in your home directory and look at its permissions.
Decide whether you will use the key from your own machine or from the server, and make the file permissions correct wherever it lives.
Log in as the next user, then read that user’s password from the location the Level Goal gives. You will need that password for the next level.
Why it matters
Passwords get guessed and phished; keys are far harder to steal remotely. Almost every cloud server and Git host uses SSH keys.

Level Goal
The password for the next level can be retrieved by submitting the password of the current level to port 30000 on localhost.
Commands you may need to solve this level
ssh, telnet, nc, openssl, s_client, nmap
Helpful Reading Material
How the Internet works in 5 minutes (YouTube) (Not completely accurate, but good enough for beginners)
IP Addresses
IP Address on Wikipedia
Localhost on Wikipedia
Ports
Port (computer networking) on Wikipedia
Study guide
Level map: logged in as bandit14, find the password for bandit15.
What this level teaches
What a network service is, and how to talk to one directly.
Key ideas
Client and server. A server listens on a port; a client connects and exchanges data. Here you are the client.
localhost (127.0.0.1) means “this very machine”, which makes it ideal for safe practice.
TCP. A reliable byte stream. Many simple protocols are just lines of text.
nc (netcat) opens a TCP connection and connects it to your keyboard and screen, so you can type to a service like a human protocol client.
How to approach it
Connect to the port the Level Goal gives.
Send the previous level’s password followed by a newline, and read the reply.
Notice that anyone on the network path could read this exchange because it is unencrypted. The next level fixes that.
Why it matters
Every protocol you know (HTTP, SMTP, Redis) is text over a port, and netcat is the debugging tool for all of them.

text: Source: This content is aggregated from overthewire (MIT). Visit the original repository for the latest version.
Level Goal
The password for the next level can be retrieved by submitting the password of the current level to port 30001 on localhost using SSL/TLS encryption.
Helpful note: Getting “DONE”, “RENEGOTIATING” or “KEYUPDATE”? Read the “CONNECTED COMMANDS” section in the manpage.
Commands you may need to solve this level
ssh, telnet, nc, ncat, socat, openssl, s_client, nmap, netstat, ss
Helpful Reading Material
Secure Socket Layer/Transport Layer Security on Wikipedia
OpenSSL Cookbook - Testing with OpenSSL
Study guide
Level map: logged in as bandit15, find the password for bandit16.
What this level teaches
TLS, the encryption layer behind HTTPS, and how to speak it by hand.
Key ideas
TLS wraps TCP. The same text conversation takes place, but inside an encrypted, authenticated channel set up by a handshake.
Certificates. A server proves its identity with a certificate. Lab servers often present self-signed ones, which openssl s_client reports but still lets you use.
openssl s_client -connect HOST:PORT is a netcat-like client for TLS.

Surprising words. If you see KEYUPDATE or RENEGOTIATING, s_client interpreted a line you sent as one of its own commands. Read the “CONNECTED COMMANDS” section of man s_client and look at the quiet-mode options.
How to approach it
Connect to the port given and inspect the certificate details it prints.
Send the password and read the reply.
Compare this with the previous level to feel the difference between plain and encrypted channels.
Why it matters
Debugging HTTPS, mail or API connections often means using openssl s_client to see what the server really presents.

text: Source: This content is aggregated from overthewire (MIT). Visit the original repository for the latest version.
Level Goal

The credentials for the next level can be retrieved by submitting the password of the current level to a port on localhost in the range 31000 to 32000. First find out which of these ports have a server listening on them. Then find out which of those speak SSL/TLS and which don’t. There is only 1 server that will give the next credentials, the others will simply send back to you whatever you send to it.
Helpful note: Getting “DONE”, “RENEGOTIATING” or “KEYUPDATE”? Read the “CONNECTED COMMANDS” section in the manpage.
Commands you may need to solve this level
ssh, telnet, nc, ncat, socat, openssl, s_client, nmap, netstat, ss
Helpful Reading Material
Port scanner on Wikipedia
Study guide
Level map: logged in as bandit16, find the credentials for bandit17.
What this level teaches
Reconnaissance: finding which services are running and what they speak.
Key ideas
Port scanning. nmap -p 31000-32000 localhost tests each port in a range to see which are open.
Service detection. Nmap’s version-detection options probe open ports to guess whether they speak TLS or plain text.
Elimination. Of the open ports, some are echo servers that repeat what you send; only one returns real credentials.
Credentials are not always passwords. Here the reward is a private key. Save it to a new directory you create under /tmp and set strict permissions before using it.
How to approach it
Scan only the range given and only localhost.
For each open port, try TLS first, then plain text, and watch the responses.
Write down which port did what; it helps you avoid repeating work.
Why it matters
Mapping a target’s attack surface is step one of every penetration test. The ethics rule applies: scan only systems you own or have written permission to test.

text: Source: This content is aggregated from overthewire (MIT). Visit the original repository for the latest version.
Level Goal

There are 2 files in the homedirectory: passwords.old and passwords.new. The password for the next level is in passwords.new and is the only line that has been changed between passwords.old and passwords.new
NOTE: if you have solved this level and see ‘Byebye!’ when trying to log into bandit18, this is related to the next level, bandit19
Commands you may need to solve this level
cat, grep, ls, diff
Study guide
Level map: logged in as bandit17, find the password for bandit18.
What this level teaches
How to find differences between two versions of a file, and how to read a diff.
Key ideas
diff old new prints only the lines that differ. A < marks a line from the first file and > a line from the second.
Why it matters for text. Version control, patches and configuration audits all rely on exactly this idea.
A hint in the Level Goal: only one line changed, so the output should be tiny.
How to approach it
Read man diff, paying attention to the default output format.
Decide which of the two lines is the password, using the file names in the Level Goal.
After you finish, log out and back in as the new user. If a message appears, it relates to the next level, so keep reading.
Why it matters
git diff, code review and configuration-drift tools are all diff under another name.

text: Source: This content is aggregated from overthewire (MIT). Visit the original repository for the latest version.
Level Goal
The password for the next level is stored in a file readme in the homedirectory. Unfortunately, someone has modified .bashrc to log you out when you log in with SSH.
Commands you may need to solve this level
ssh, ls, cat
Study guide
Level map: logged in as bandit18, find the password for bandit19.
What this level teaches
That an SSH login is not the only way to run something on a server, and what shell startup files do.
Key ideas
.bashrc. A script that bash reads when it starts, used to customise your shell. Whoever controls it controls what happens at login, and attackers abuse that for persistence.
Interactive vs command mode. ssh user@host opens an interactive shell, but ssh user@host COMMAND runs one command and returns.
Read the argument description in man ssh to see how the command is passed.
How to approach it
Try logging in normally and observe what the modified .bashrc does.
Use the remote-command form of ssh to run ls first, then cat the file the Level Goal mentions.
Why it matters
Automation tools such as Ansible, deployment scripts and Git over SSH all run commands remotely this way.

text: Source: This content is aggregated from overthewire (MIT). Visit the original repository for the latest version.
Level Goal
The password for the next level is stored in a file called - located in the home directory
Commands you may need to solve this level
ls , cd , cat , file , du , find
Helpful Reading Material
Google Search for “dashed filename”
Advanced Bash-scripting Guide - Chapter 3 - Special Characters
Study guide
Level map: logged in as bandit1, find the password for bandit2.
What this level teaches
Why some filenames break commands, and how to talk to a command about a file that looks like an option.
Key ideas
Options start with a dash. cat -n file means “number the lines”. A bare - is conventionally “standard input”, so a command that receives only - does not see a file at all.
The shell passes arguments through unchanged. It is the program, not the shell, that decides - is special.
Two standard remedies exist: make the argument unmistakably a path, or tell the program that options have ended. Both are described in the man pages of nearly every command.
How to approach it
Run ls and notice the odd filename. Try cat on it and observe what happens; failing on purpose is a good way to learn.
Think about how to write a path that does not begin with a dash. The current directory has a short name you already know.
Search man cat or man bash for the “end of options” convention, which is useful for every command you will ever use.
Why it matters

Attackers deliberately create files whose names look like command-line flags, which can trick scripts that run rm * or tar * into executing options. Knowing the mechanism is how you defend against it.

text: Source: This content is aggregated from overthewire (MIT). Visit the original repository for the latest version.
Level Goal

To gain access to the next level, you should use the setuid binary in the homedirectory. Execute it without arguments to find out how to use it. The password for this level can be found in the usual place (/etc/bandit_pass), after you have used the setuid binary.
Helpful Reading Material
setuid on Wikipedia
Study guide
Level map: logged in as bandit19, find the password for bandit20.
What this level teaches
How Unix lets a program run with its owner’s privileges, and why that is both useful and dangerous.
Key ideas
User IDs. A process has a real UID (who started it) and an effective UID (whose permissions it uses for access checks).
setuid. When a file has the setuid bit (shown as s in ls -l), running it makes the effective UID the file’s owner. The classic example is passwd, which lets ordinary users update a root-owned file.
id prints your current user and group IDs.
Boundary. Every setuid program is a deliberate crack in the privilege wall, so it must be written very carefully.
How to approach it
Look at the binary with ls -l and note the s.
Run it with no arguments, as the Level Goal suggests, and read how it wants to be used.
The password then sits in the usual place under /etc/bandit_pass.
Why it matters
Hunting for setuid binaries (find / -perm -4000) is a standard step in Linux privilege escalation, both for attackers and for hardening audits.

text: Source: This content is aggregated from overthewire (MIT). Visit the original repository for the latest version.
Level Goal

There is a setuid binary in the homedirectory that does the following: it makes a connection to localhost on the port you specify as a commandline argument. It then reads a line of text from the connection and compares it to the password in the previous level (bandit20). If the password is correct, it will transmit the password for the next level (bandit21).
NOTE: Try connecting to your own network daemon to see if it works as you think
Commands you may need to solve this level
ssh, nc, cat, bash, screen, tmux, Unix ‘job control’ (bg, fg, jobs, &, CTRL-Z, …)
Study guide
Level map: logged in as bandit20, find the password for bandit21.
What this level teaches
Reversing the client and server roles, and juggling several things at once in one terminal.
Key ideas
Listening. nc -l PORT waits for someone to connect (the exact syntax varies between netcat versions, so check man nc). Think of it as building a tiny server by hand.
The role flip. This time the setuid program is the client; you provide the server.
Job control. Press Ctrl-Z to suspend a command, bg to continue it in the background, fg to bring it back, jobs to list. Adding & at the end of a command starts it in the background.
Alternatives. A second SSH session, tmux or screen solve the same problem by giving you multiple terminals.
How to approach it
Start a listener that will send the current password to whatever connects.
Launch the setuid program pointing at your listener’s port.
Read what the program sends back; as the Level Goal says, test your listener on its own first to be sure it behaves as you expect.
Why it matters
Reverse connections, callbacks and test servers are everyday techniques for debugging networks and, in security, for understanding how malware communicates.

text: Source: This content is aggregated from overthewire (MIT). Visit the original repository for the latest version.
Level Goal
A program is running automatically at regular intervals from cron, the time-based job scheduler. Look in /etc/cron.d/ for the configuration and see what command is being executed.
Commands you may need to solve this level
cron, crontab, crontab(5) (use “man 5 crontab” to access this)
Study guide
Level map: logged in as bandit21, find the password for bandit22.
What this level teaches
How Linux schedules recurring work, and why reading someone else’s script is a security skill.
Key ideas
cron is a daemon that runs commands at scheduled times. System-wide entries live in /etc/cron.d/.
Crontab syntax. Five time fields (minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week) followed by the user and the command. man 5 crontab explains each field.
Whose permissions? A cron job runs as the user named in its entry, which may not be you.
Follow the data. The job’s script reads something and writes it somewhere; your job is to see where.
How to approach it
List /etc/cron.d/ and read the entry for the next user.
Open the script it runs and trace, line by line, what it reads and where it writes.
Go and look at the output location.
Why it matters
Cron is a favourite place for misconfigurations that expose data or allow privilege escalation, and attackers also use it for persistence.
docs/wargames/bandit/bandit22/index.html.title: Bandit Level 22 | Wargames

text: Source: This content is aggregated from overthewire (MIT). Visit the original repository for the latest version.
Level Goal
A program is running automatically at regular intervals from cron, the time-based job scheduler. Look in /etc/cron.d/ for the configuration and see what command is being executed.

NOTE: Looking at shell scripts written by other people is a very useful skill. The script for this level is intentionally made easy to read. If you are having problems understanding what it does, try executing it to see the debug information it prints.
Commands you may need to solve this level
cron, crontab, crontab(5) (use “man 5 crontab” to access this)
Study guide
Level map: logged in as bandit22, find the password for bandit23.
What this level teaches
Reading shell scripts critically, including who a script runs as.
Key ideas
Command substitution. $(command) replaces itself with that command’s output, so scripts can build names or values on the fly.
Identity. whoami prints the current user. A script run by cron reports the cron entry’s user, not yours.
Hashing. md5sum turns any text into a fixed-length fingerprint. A script can use it to derive an unguessable-looking filename from a known string.
Debugging. The Level Goal suggests running the script to see its debug output; try each piece in the terminal individually.
How to approach it
Read the script slowly and write in your notes what each line does.
Ask: what value does whoami return when cron runs it, and what string gets hashed?
Reproduce that computation yourself, then look where the script saved its result.
Why it matters
“Security through an obscure filename” fails once the algorithm is visible. Auditing scripts and spotting such patterns is routine code-review work.

text: Source: This content is aggregated from overthewire (MIT). Visit the original repository for the latest version.
Level Goal
A program is running automatically at regular intervals from cron, the time-based job scheduler. Look in /etc/cron.d/ for the configuration and see what command is being executed.
NOTE: This level requires you to create your own first shell-script. This is a very big step and you should be proud of yourself when you beat this level!
NOTE 2: Keep in mind that your shell script is removed once executed, so you may want to keep a copy around…
Commands you may need to solve this level
chmod, cron, crontab, crontab(5) (use “man 5 crontab” to access this)
Study guide
Level map: logged in as bandit23, find the password for bandit24.
What this level teaches
Writing a script, and the danger of a privileged job that executes files other users can write.
Key ideas
Shebang. The first line #!/bin/bash tells the system which interpreter runs the file.
Executable bit. chmod +x makes the script runnable; the cron user must also be able to read and run it.
Drop directories. Some jobs run every file placed in a directory, then delete it. Whoever can write to that directory can run code as the job’s user.
Permissions on your workspace. The job runs as a different user, so the place where it writes output must allow that.
How to approach it
Read the cron entry and its script and identify which directory it executes and who runs it.
Write a tiny script that copies the target password somewhere you can read it, test it by hand, and keep a spare copy because the job deletes the original.
Wait for the next scheduled run (check the schedule), then collect the result.
Why it matters
This is a textbook privilege-escalation pattern: a root-run cron or service that executes files from a world-writable location.

text: Source: This content is aggregated from overthewire (MIT). Visit the original repository for the latest version.
Level Goal

A daemon is listening on port 30002 and will give you the password for bandit25 if given the password for bandit24 and a secret numeric 4-digit pincode. There is no way to retrieve the pincode except by going through all of the 10000 combinations, called brute-forcing.
You do not need to create new connections each time
Study guide
Level map: logged in as bandit24, find the password for bandit25.
What this level teaches
How brute force works, when it is feasible, and how to automate it with a shell loop.
Key ideas
Search space. A four-digit PIN has 10,000 possibilities; at that size, exhaustive search is practical.
Loops. Shell for loops, seq and printf can generate every candidate, and printf '%04d' pads with leading zeros (so 7 becomes 0007).
One connection. The Level Goal says you do not need a new connection for each guess, so you can pipe the whole stream into a single nc.
Defences. Rate limiting, lockouts and longer secrets exist precisely to make this attack impractical.
How to approach it
Test the protocol by hand with a few guesses to learn the exact input format.
Generate all 10,000 lines of the form the service expects, then send them in one go.
Filter the output so only the successful reply stands out.
Why it matters
Understanding the arithmetic of brute force explains why short PINs, weak passwords and unthrottled login forms are dangerous.

text: Source: This content is aggregated from overthewire (MIT). Visit the original repository for the latest version.
Level Goal
Logging in to bandit26 from bandit25 should be fairly easy… The shell for user bandit26 is not /bin/bash, but something else. Find out what it is, how it works and how to break out of it.
NOTE: if you’re a Windows user and typically use Powershell to ssh into bandit: Powershell is known to cause issues with the intended solution to this level. You should use command prompt instead.
Commands you may need to solve this level
ssh, cat, more, vi, ls, id, pwd
Study guide
Level map: logged in as bandit25, gain an interactive shell as bandit26.
What this level teaches
How login shells work, and that many ordinary programs have built-in escape hatches.
Key ideas
Login shell. The final field of each line in /etc/passwd names the program run at login. It need not be a shell, and it can be a program that lets you do only one thing.
Pagers. more shows text one screenful at a time. Interactive pagers and editors such as vi can launch commands, edit files and change settings, which makes them valuable stepping stones.
Terminal size matters. A pager only pauses when output is taller than your window, so the size of the window affects what you can do.
GTFOBins. A public catalogue of normal Unix programs that can be abused to escape restrictions.
How to approach it
Look at the shell recorded for bandit26 and read what that program does.
Think about what happens if the output is longer than your terminal, and what you can do in that state.
From inside an editor, remember that it can run commands and change the shell it uses.
If you use Windows, run ssh from Command Prompt rather than PowerShell, as the Level Goal advises.
Why it matters
Restricted shells, kiosk systems and sudo rules that permit “just one safe command” are all defeated by this kind of escape.

What this level teaches
Deleting something from the latest version of a repository does not delete it from history.
Key ideas
Commits are snapshots. Each commit records the full state of the project and a message describing the change.
git log lists commits; git show and git diff display what a commit changed.
Leaked secrets persist. Credentials committed once remain recoverable from earlier commits even after a “fix” commit.

Read the commit log, paying attention to commit messages that suggest something was fixed or removed.
Inspect those earlier commits to see exactly what they changed.
Why it matters

Level Goal

Level map: logged in as bandit2, find the password for bandit3.
What this level teaches
How the shell splits a command line into words, and how to keep a filename with spaces together.
Key ideas
Word splitting. The shell breaks a command at every space, so cat my file is read as two arguments, my and file.
Quoting (single or double quotes) and backslash escaping both tell the shell “treat this as one word”.
Tab completion has the shell finish a name for you, inserting the correct escapes automatically.

ls shows the file. Note how its name appears.
Try the three techniques above on a harmless file first, for example one you create yourself in a mktemp -d directory.
Start typing the name and press Tab. Seeing the escapes the shell inserts is the quickest way to understand them.

Spaces and special characters in filenames cause the classic scripting bugs. Always quoting variables in scripts ("$file") comes directly from this lesson.

Git branches, and how to see work that is not on the default branch.
Key ideas
Branches are named, movable pointers to lines of development. A clone checks out only the default branch at first.
Remote branches. git branch -a lists local and remote branches; git checkout switches to one.
Log per branch. git log shows only the history reachable from the branch you are on.

git tag lists them and git show TAG displays what each points to.
Searching a repo. When files and logs reveal nothing, enumerate every kind of reference Git keeps.

git
Helpful Reading Material
Installing Git
Git from the Bottom Up
Study guide
Level map: using the password for bandit31, find the password for bandit32.
What this level teaches
Pushing to a remote, and how ignore rules and server-side hooks work.
Key ideas
The three areas. Working tree, staging area (git add) and repository (git commit) are separate; git push then sends commits to the remote.
.gitignore. A list of patterns Git deliberately skips. If a file you need to add matches a pattern, Git silently refuses unless you force it.
Server hooks. A remote can run a script when it receives a push and send messages back to you. Read the output of git push carefully.
Read the README. It states exactly what the remote expects.
How to approach it
Clone, then read the README to learn what file and content the server wants.
Create it, try to add and commit it, and diagnose why Git skips it.
Push and read what the server prints back.
Why it matters
Hooks drive continuous integration, deployments and policy checks, and understanding what git add actually does stops “my change disappeared” confusion.

Level Goal
After all this git stuff, it’s time for another escape. Good luck!
Commands you may need to solve this level

Study guide
Level map: logged in as bandit32, find the password for bandit33.
What this level teaches
How shell parameters and expansions work, by being forced to use only characters that survive uppercase conversion.
Key ideas
Commands are case-sensitive. LS is not ls, so a shell that upper-cases input rejects normal commands.
Special parameters. The shell defines variables such as the name of the running shell and the number of arguments. These are written with symbols and digits that uppercase conversion cannot change.
Expansions replace such a parameter with its value before the command runs, so you can obtain a lowercase command indirectly.
Read the “Special Parameters” section of man bash.
How to approach it
Log in and observe exactly what the restricted program does to your input.
Search the bash manual for parameters that are not letters.
Think about what program that parameter’s value would run, and what you could do from there.
Why it matters
Input filters and blocklists are routinely bypassed by features of the interpreter behind them. This is the mindset behind many web and shell injection techniques.

Level Goal
The password for the next level is stored in a hidden file in the inhere directory.
Commands you may need to solve this level
ls , cd , cat , file , du , find
Study guide
Level map: logged in as bandit3, find the password for bandit4.
What this level teaches
How Unix hides files, and why that is a convention rather than a security feature.
Key ideas
Dotfiles. Any file or directory whose name starts with . is skipped by a plain ls. They typically hold per-user configuration such as .bashrc or .ssh/.
ls -a shows “all” entries, including . (this directory) and .. (the parent).
Hidden is not secret. Anyone can list the files; the dot only reduces clutter.
How to approach it
Enter the inhere directory. A plain ls appears empty, which is the clue.
Use the option that includes hidden entries, then print the file that is not . or ...
Combine options such as -la to also see permissions and sizes.
Why it matters
Malware and attackers often hide persistence in dotfiles, and incident responders list them first. You will also meet dotfiles daily when configuring tools.

text: Source: This content is aggregated from overthewire (MIT). Visit the original repository for the latest version.
Level Goal
The password for the next level is stored in the only human-readable file in the inhere directory. Tip: if your terminal is messed up, try the “reset” command.
Commands you may need to solve this level
ls , cd , cat , file , du , find
Study guide
Level map: logged in as bandit4, find the password for bandit5.
What this level teaches
A filename or extension tells you nothing reliable about contents. The file command inspects the data itself.
Key ideas
Magic numbers. Many file formats begin with signature bytes. file reads them and reports a type such as ASCII text, data or executable.
Why printing binary files hurts. Sending arbitrary bytes to a terminal can send control codes that garble your display. If that happens, the reset command restores it.
Filenames can still be awkward. The files in this directory begin with a character that already caused trouble in an earlier level.
How to approach it
List the directory, then run file on every candidate at once using a wildcard. Remember how Level 2 told you to write the paths.
Only cat the file that file identifies as text.
Why it matters
Forensics, malware triage and upload filters all rely on content-based identification rather than trusting names, a theme that returns strongly in the web-security game Natas.

text: Source: This content is aggregated from overthewire (MIT). Visit the original repository for the latest version.
Level Goal
The password for the next level is stored in a file somewhere under the inhere directory and has all of the following properties:
human-readable
1033 bytes in size
not executable
Commands you may need to solve this level
ls , cd , cat , file , du , find
Study guide
Level map: logged in as bandit5, find the password for bandit6.
What this level teaches
Searching a directory tree by properties instead of by name, with find.
Key ideas
find PATH tests walks a tree and prints entries matching every test you list. Tests include -type f (regular files), -size and -executable.
Size units matter. In -size, a suffix selects the unit and a missing suffix means 512-byte blocks, not bytes. Check man find for the byte suffix before trusting a result.
Negation. A leading ! inverts a test, which is how you say “not executable”.
Tests are combined with an implicit AND.
How to approach it
Start broad (find inhere -type f) and add one test at a time, watching the output shrink.
When exactly one file remains, check it with file before reading it.
Why it matters
Locating files by size, owner or modification time is core incident-response work, for example finding recently changed files or unexpected setuid binaries.

text: Source: This content is aggregated from overthewire (MIT). Visit the original repository for the latest version.

Commands you may need to solve this level

Study guide
Level map: logged in as bandit6, find the password for bandit7.
What this level teaches
Using find on the entire filesystem with ownership filters, and handling the flood of “Permission denied” messages that results.
Key ideas
Ownership. Every file has an owning user and group; find can filter on both with -user and -group.
Standard streams. Programs write results to stdout (file descriptor 1) and errors to stderr (2). Redirecting stderr with 2>/dev/null discards the noise without hiding results.
/dev/null is a special file that swallows everything written to it.
Search scope. Starting from / means every directory you cannot read produces an error.
How to approach it
Combine ownership and size tests, starting your search at /.
Redirect only stderr, so genuine results stay visible.
Read the single remaining match.
Why it matters
Tracking down files by owner is how administrators audit permissions, and redirection is the basis of every shell pipeline you will write.

text: Source: This content is aggregated from overthewire (MIT). Visit the original repository for the latest version.
Bandit

The Bandit wargame is aimed at absolute beginners. It will teach the basics needed to be able to play other wargames. If you notice something essential is missing or have ideas for new levels, please let us know!
Note for beginners

This game, like most other games, is organised in levels. You start at Level 0 and try to “beat” or “finish” it. Finishing a level results in information on how to start the next level. The pages on this website for “Level <X>” contain information on how to start level X from the previous level. E.g. The page for Level 1 has information on how to gain access from Level 0 to Level 1. All levels in this game have a page on this website, and they are all linked to from the sidemenu on the left of this page.

You will encounter many situations in which you have no idea what you are supposed to do. Don’t panic! Don’t give up! The purpose of this game is for you to learn the basics. Part of learning the basics, is reading a lot of new information. If you’ve never used the command line before, a good first read is this introduction to user commands.
There are several things you can try when you are unsure how to continue:

First, if you know a command, but don’t know how to use it, try the manual (man page) by entering man <command>. For example, man ls to learn about the “ls” command. The “man” command also has a manual, try it! When using man, press q to quit (you can also use / and n and N to search).
Second, if there is no man page, the command might be a shell built-in. In that case use the “help <X>” command. E.g. help cd
Also, your favorite search-engine is your friend. Learn how to use it! I recommend Google.
Lastly, if you are still stuck, you can join us via chat
You’re ready to start! Begin with Level 0, linked at the left of this page. Good luck!

Note for VMs: You may fail to connect to overthewire.org via SSH with a “broken pipe error” when the network adapter for the VM is configured to use NAT mode. Adding the setting IPQoS throughput to /etc/ssh/ssh_config should resolve the issue. If this does not solve your issue, the only option then is to change the adapter to Bridged mode.
Study guide
This guide is spoiler-free: it explains what each stretch of Bandit teaches and how to get unstuck, but it never lists passwords or finished solutions. The struggle is where the learning happens.
What Bandit teaches

Bandit is a guided tour of the Unix command line. You begin with a single SSH login and finish by chaining small tools, scripting, scheduling jobs, abusing misconfigured permissions and escaping restricted shells. Nothing needs programming experience; every level can be solved with standard tools that ship on any Linux system.
How the levels are numbered

Each level page describes how to get to that level from the one before it. The page titled Level 1 is therefore done while logged in as bandit0, and its result is the password for bandit1. The study guide on each page repeats this as a “Level map” line so you never have to count.
The learning path
Levels
Theme
Core skills
First steps
SSH, ls, cat, files with awkward names
Finding things
hidden files, file, find, permissions and ownership
Text and encodings
grep, sort, uniq, strings, Base64, ROT13, compression
Keys and networks
SSH keys, ports, nc, TLS with openssl, port scanning
Identity and privilege
diff, remote commands, setuid binaries, job control
Automation
cron, shell scripting, brute force
Escaping shells
restricted login shells, more/vi escape hatches
Git
clone, history, branches, tags, push hooks
Last escape
breaking out of a hostile shell
Tools worth knowing before you start
man — the built-in manual. Press / to search and q to quit. Reading man pages is the single most useful habit Bandit builds.
ssh, scp — remote shell and file copy.
grep, find, sort, uniq, tr, diff — the text-processing core.
nc (netcat), openssl, nmap — network clients and scanners.
git — needed on your own machine for Levels 28–32.
Study habits that pay off
Keep a notes file on your own machine: password, command that worked, and one sentence on why. Passwords are not saved for you and occasionally change.
Predict the output of a command before you run it. Surprises are where the learning is.
When stuck, shrink the problem: run each command in a pipeline separately and look at what each stage produces.
Work in a private directory under /tmp made with mktemp -d whenever you need to create files; you usually cannot write to your home directory.
Be a good neighbour. Other players share the server, so clean up temporary files and never hunt for other people’s work.
After Bandit

The suggested order on the games index is Bandit first, then any of Natas (web), Krypton (cryptography) or Leviathan (reverse engineering), then the binary-exploitation games Narnia, Behemoth and onward.

What this level teaches
How the PATH environment variable and the current directory influence which program gets executed.
Key ideas
Commands run by name. When a program calls a command without an absolute path, the system searches the directories in PATH in order.
Controlling the search. If you can put your own program earlier in that search, your program runs with the caller’s privileges.
Trace to see the call. strace and ltrace show exactly what the program executes and in which directory it works.
Writable workspace. Make a private directory under /tmp for your files.

Trace the program and note every command it runs by name.
Think about what a replacement for that command should do with its privileges.
Make it findable and run the original program.

Unsafe use of system() and relative commands in setuid programs is a long-standing source of privilege escalation.

Behemoth
Don’t let behemoth get the better of you.
Behemoth is a wargame that has been rescued from the demise of intruded.net, previously hosted on behemoth.intruded.net. Big thanks to adc, morla and reth for their help in resurrecting this game!
What follows below is the original description of behemoth, copied from intruded.net:

Summary: Difficulty: 3/10 Levels: 9 Platform: Linux/x86 Author: Anders Tonfeldt Special Thanks: Description: This wargame deals with a lot of regular vulnerabilities found commonly 'out in the wild'. While the game makes no attempts at emulating a real environment it will teach you how to exploit several of the most common coding mistakes including buffer overflows, race conditions and privilege escalation.
Behemoth’s levels are called behemoth0, behemoth1, … etc. and can be accessed on behemoth.labs.overthewire.org through SSH on port 2221.
To login to the first level use:
Username: behemoth0 Password: behemoth0
Data for the levels can be found in /behemoth/.
Study guide
This guide is spoiler-free: it explains what Behemoth expects of you and how to work, but never gives passwords or finished exploits.
What Behemoth teaches

The original description from intruded.net says the game deals with regular vulnerabilities commonly found “out in the wild” and, while it makes no attempt to emulate a real environment, teaches several of the most common coding mistakes including buffer overflows, race conditions and privilege escalation. The authors rated it 3 out of 10, on Linux/x86, and Utumno’s authors call it a little easier than their own game.
Connecting

Behemoth is rescued from the defunct intruded.net, thanks to adc, morla and reth. Connect with SSH to behemoth.labs.overthewire.org on port 2221. The first account is behemoth0 with the password behemoth0. Data for the levels is in /behemoth/, and each level’s password is in /etc/behemoth_pass/, readable only by that level’s user.
How the levels are numbered
The page for Level N is the account you are logged in as. You are behemothN and you are looking for the password for behemothN+1. The upstream pages deliberately say nothing more.
How it differs from Narnia
Narnia hands you the C source. Behemoth gives you the compiled program, so you must learn what it does from tracing and disassembly before you can exploit it.
A reconnaissance checklist
ls -l /behemoth/ and look at the permissions. A setuid bit marks the program as your route to the next user.
file and strings on the binary.
Run it normally, then with odd input.
ltrace and strace for library and system calls.
gdb or objdump -d for the logic.
Decide what kind of bug you are looking at before choosing an exploit.
Tools
gdb (optionally with a helper like gef or pwndbg), objdump, ltrace, strace, ghidra, gcc, nc, pwntools, and a notes file.
Where this fits
The recommended order is Bandit, one of Natas, Krypton or Leviathan, Narnia, then Behemoth, then Utumno and Maze.

You can see the reply. That is what makes a leak possible: format specifiers print stack values back to you.
Direct parameter access. The %N$x syntax reads the Nth argument directly, so you can scan the stack without writing hundreds of specifiers.

Use the debug service to understand the stack layout, then repeat on the real one.
Leak the values you need, compute addresses, and design the write.
Script the exploit so you can rerun it against a fresh address space.

Info leaks plus a write primitive are the building blocks of nearly every modern exploit chain.

About

Blacksun is a PullThePlug / OverTheWire wargame that is meant to help people learn more advanced exploitation techniques against hardened hosts and environments. It is implemented by PaX patches, and the Hardened Gentoo project. It is a work in process If you have any questions you can contact andrewg via email.

Blacksun is not an exploit novice’s game / toolset, as it assumes a bunch of previous knowledge, such as programming, format string exploitation, heap exploitation, shellcoding, and out of the box thinking, amongst other things. However, PullThePlug / OverTheWire does have another wargame that’s a lot easier, but still quite challenging available here.

Also, it is not meant to discredit any of the work that has been done towards PaX (hi pipacs!), as it is quite awesome. Perhaps even it will lead to better defensive, and maybe better offensive techniques. And most likely greater understanding with the issues involved.
Aims
Blacksun is aimed towards demonstrating and helping people better understand:
Address space randomisation
Non executable memory and things that affect it
Stack smashing prevention
Information leaks
Code auditing and identifying code paths and vulnerable constructs
Being able to construct the exploitation environment
Binary auditing, and differencing
Access control list systems
Reading material

Study guide
This guide explains what the Blacksun material covers and how to study it. The game is currently offline, so these pages are best read as a curriculum rather than a live challenge.

What Blacksun teaches

Blacksun targets players who already know programming, format-string exploitation, heap exploitation and shellcoding. It is built on PaX patches and Hardened Gentoo, so the exploits you have practised on easier systems will not simply work. The stated aims are to understand:
Address space layout randomisation (ASLR)
Non-executable memory and what weakens it
Stack-smashing prevention
Information leaks
Code auditing and identifying vulnerable code paths
Building the exploitation environment
Binary auditing and differencing

Drifter can be accessed on drifter.labs.overthewire.org via SSH on port 2230. Level 0 listens on port 1111.
Level0 is an extremely trivial, encrypted, remote syscall proxy. Your aim is to read the contents of a file called “drifter0.password” to get the password for user drifter0.

Upon connection, it sets up an encrypted rc4 key (based on the connecting IP address / port), read()’s in 9 integers, and then decrypts them, and handles them off to syscall(). This allows the network client to execute arbitrary syscalls in a safe way.
To give you an idea of what’s needed:
You’ll need to
If you are behind a NAT/PAT, you might want to do vortex level0, and complete this level from vortex, as otherwise your known IP address and port information changes.
Examine how the RC4 keys are generated, and how they are applied
mmap2() some memory. You will get the address where the memory was allocated in the response from the server. mmap2() takes its arguments from registers, not the stack.

read() into that allocated buffer to get the file name. The source fd that you need will be 4. (0-2 = stdin/stdout/stderr, 3 will be network socket, so 4 in next in line. You will want to read in enough data for the filename “instructions”
Write the filename (“instructions” sans quotes) to the allocated memory location to your client socket
open() the “instructions” file. You will get the fd it was allocated to in response
read() from the allocated file descriptor to your allocated memory
write() from the allocated buffer to the socket on the server (fd 4)
Once all that is done, you will have the contents of the instructions file printed to your screen.

Understanding syscalls demystifies shellcode, sandboxes and tools like strace.

Drifter
Drifter is a wargame along the lines of Vortex.
Study guide
This guide explains what each Drifter level asks for, based on the level pages, without passwords or finished exploits.
What Drifter teaches

The upstream description is one sentence: Drifter is a wargame along the lines of Vortex. Its levels use the same toolkit — network clients, stack and heap exploitation, format strings, reverse engineering and cryptanalysis — but on a different mix of targets, including remote daemons, C++ code, third-party libraries and ASLR-protected binaries.
Connecting

Drifter is reached with SSH at drifter.labs.overthewire.org on port 2230. Level 0 is a network service that listens on port 1111. Source code for several levels is provided under /drifter/ (for example drifter0_src, drifter3_src and drifter14_src).
Prerequisites

Finish Bandit, Narnia and Behemoth, and ideally the early Vortex levels. The Drifter Level 0 page even suggests doing Vortex Level 0 first, to have a stable machine to work from if you are behind NAT.
The skills ladder
Levels
Theme
Core skills
Remote system-call proxy
RC4, raw syscalls, a custom client
Memory corruption
C++ vtables, stack overflow quirks, old heap allocators
Analysis and logic
reverse engineering, resource limits, game logic
Remote daemons
format strings, disassembly, custom shellcode
Privileges and practice
file formats, non-executable stacks
Randomisation and reversing
ASLR, RPC-style protocols
Open-ended
unexpected approaches, third-party library bugs, decompression
Tools
gdb, objdump, ltrace/strace, a disassembler (the Level 7 page mentions IDA Free), gcc, pwntools, Python and C for network clients.
Habits that help
Read the source where it is given before touching the binary.
Script everything; remote exploits need many attempts.
Keep a record of addresses and offsets, as they differ between levels and sometimes between runs.

Krypton
The Krypton wargame.
Study guide
This guide is spoiler-free: it explains the cryptography each level introduces and how to attack it in principle, but it never gives passwords or ready-made solutions.
What Krypton teaches

Krypton is a short course in how classical ciphers are broken and why modern ones are built the way they are. Each level gives you a ciphertext (and sometimes a tool) and asks you to recover the next password. You will see substitution ciphers, polyalphabetic ciphers, known-plaintext attacks and finally a stream cipher with a weak random number generator.
How to play

You log in over SSH to krypton.labs.overthewire.org on port 2231 as krypton1, using the password you derive from Level 0. The files for each level are in /krypton/, and the password for the next level is in a file named after it (for example krypton2). Because you cannot write in most places, create a working directory under /tmp with mktemp -d.
How the levels are numbered
Level 0 contains the first password in encoded form. After that, the page for Level N tells you how to decrypt the file that holds the password for Level N+1.
The skills ladder
Level
Theme
Core idea
Encoding
Base64 is reversible and not secret
Rotation ciphers
ROT13 and the Caesar cipher
Chosen plaintext
an encryption oracle reveals the key
Frequency analysis
monoalphabetic substitution with several messages
Polyalphabetic
Vigenère with a known key length
Polyalphabetic
Vigenère with an unknown key length
Stream ciphers
XOR keystreams and a weak random generator
Key concepts
Plaintext, ciphertext, key. The message, the scrambled form and the secret that controls scrambling.
Substitution vs transposition. Replacing symbols versus rearranging them.
Frequency analysis. In English, letters appear with predictable frequencies (E, T, A, O are common), and these survive monoalphabetic substitution.
Kerckhoffs’s principle. A cipher must stay secure even if everything about it, except the key, is public.
One-time pad. A truly random key as long as the message and never reused is provably unbreakable, but impractical for most uses.
Tools
tr, fold, sort, uniq -c, bc, Python, and graphical tools such as CrypTool. A spreadsheet or a short script for counting letters makes the middle levels much faster.
Where this fits
Krypton is one of the three games suggested after Bandit. Its ideas return in Natas (for example the XOR cookie) and in any later work on authentication and encryption.

Base64 is an encoding, not a cipher. Anyone can undo it.
Key ideas
Encoding vs encryption. Encoding changes representation for transport. Encryption uses a secret key so that only someone with the key can read the data.
Recognising Base64. It uses letters, digits, + and /, and often ends with = padding.
Decoding tool. The base64 command with its decode option, or any programming language, reverses it.

Use the result as the password for the krypton1 account on the stated host and port.
Look around /krypton/ to see where each later level’s files live.

Tokens and credentials in Base64 are often mistaken for encrypted data. Treat the format as public.

Level Info

The password for level 2 is in the file ‘krypton2’. It is ‘encrypted’ using a simple rotation. It is also in non-standard ciphertext format. When using alpha characters for cipher text it is normal to group the letters into 5 letter clusters, regardless of word boundaries. This helps obfuscate any patterns. This file has kept the plain text word boundaries and carried them to the cipher text. Enjoy!
Study guide
Level map: logged in as krypton1, decrypt the file that holds the password for krypton2.
What this level teaches
How a rotation cipher works and how to reverse it with the tr command.
Key ideas
Rotation. Each letter is shifted a fixed number of places along the alphabet. ROT13 shifts by 13, which is self-inverse.
Keeping word boundaries. The page notes that the usual five-letter grouping has not been used here, so the ciphertext keeps the spaces of the original text.
tr. Translates one set of characters into another, as in Bandit Level 12. Work out the mapping for both upper and lower case.
How to approach it
Read the ciphertext and note that it has the shape of ordinary text.
Build the tr sets that undo the rotation described in the page.
Test on a short word you encode yourself.
Why it matters
Rotation ciphers are weak because there is nothing secret: the algorithm is the key. The same flaw reappears in less obvious forms.

text: Source: This content is aggregated from overthewire (MIT). Visit the original repository for the latest version.
Level Info
ROT13 is a simple substitution cipher.

Substitution ciphers are a simple replacement algorithm. In this example of a substitution cipher, we will explore a ‘monoalphebetic’ cipher. Monoalphebetic means, literally, “one alphabet” and you will see why.
This level contains an old form of cipher called a ‘Caesar Cipher’. A Caesar cipher shifts the alphabet by a set number. For example:
plain: a b c d e f g h i j k ... cipher: G H I J K L M N O P Q ...
In this example, the letter ‘a’ in plaintext is replaced by a ‘G’ in the ciphertext so, for example, the plaintext ‘bad’ becomes ‘HGJ’ in ciphertext.

The password for level 3 is in the file krypton3. It is in 5 letter group ciphertext. It is encrypted with a Caesar Cipher. Without any further information, this cipher text may be difficult to break. You do not have direct access to the key, however you do have access to a program that will encrypt anything you wish to give it using the key. If you think logically, this is completely easy.
One shot can solve it!
Have fun.
Additional Information:

The encrypt binary will look for the keyfile in your current working directory. Therefore, it might be best to create a working direcory in /tmp and in there a link to the keyfile. As the encrypt binary runs setuid krypton3, you also need to give krypton3 access to your working directory.
Here is an example:

krypton2@melinda:~$ mktemp -d /tmp/tmp.Wf2OnCpCDQ krypton2@melinda:~$ cd /tmp/tmp.Wf2OnCpCDQ krypton2@melinda:/tmp/tmp.Wf2OnCpCDQ$ ln -s /krypton/krypton2/keyfile.dat krypton2@melinda:/tmp/tmp.Wf2OnCpCDQ$ ls keyfile.dat krypton2@melinda:/tmp/tmp.Wf2OnCpCDQ$ chmod 777 . krypton2@melinda:/tmp/tmp.Wf2OnCpCDQ$ /krypton/krypton2/encrypt /etc/issue krypton2@melinda:/tmp/tmp.Wf2OnCpCDQ$ ls ciphertext keyfile.dat
Study guide
Level map: logged in as krypton2, decrypt the file that holds the password for krypton3.
What this level teaches
A chosen-plaintext attack: if you can make a system encrypt text of your choice, you can learn its key.
Key ideas
Caesar cipher. A substitution cipher where the alphabet is shifted by a fixed amount, here with an unknown shift.
Encryption oracle. The encrypt program encrypts anything you give it using the secret key.
Chosen plaintext. Encrypting the full alphabet once shows exactly how every letter is transformed, which is enough to decrypt anything.

Practical setup. The program looks for its key file in your current directory and runs as the next user, so it needs a working directory under /tmp with a link to the key and permissive directory permissions. The page walks you through an example.
How to approach it
Follow the setup in the page text to be able to run encrypt.
Think about the smallest, most informative input to encrypt.
Use what you learn to build the reverse mapping and apply it to the password file.
Why it matters
Any system that lets attackers encrypt, decrypt or sign arbitrary data is an oracle. Many real attacks, from padding oracles to the ECB cut-and-paste in Natas, use this idea.

text: Source: This content is aggregated from overthewire (MIT). Visit the original repository for the latest version.
Level Info
Well done. You’ve moved past an easy substitution cipher.

The main weakness of a simple substitution cipher is repeated use of a simple key. In the previous exercise you were able to introduce arbitrary plaintext to expose the key. In this example, the cipher mechanism is not available to you, the attacker.
However, you have been lucky. You have intercepted more than one message. The password to the next level is found in the file ‘krypton4’. You have also found 3 other files. (found1, found2, found3)
You know the following important details:
The message plaintexts are in American English (*** very important) - They were produced from the same key (*** even better!)
Enjoy.
Study guide
Level map: logged in as krypton3, decrypt the file that holds the password for krypton4.
What this level teaches
Frequency analysis, the classic attack on monoalphabetic substitution ciphers.
Key ideas
Same key, many messages. The page tells you the plaintexts are American English and were encrypted with the same key. More text means more reliable statistics.
Letter frequencies. Count how often each ciphertext letter appears and match the ranking against English: E, T, A, O, I, N are most common.
Patterns beyond single letters. Common words (THE, AND), common digraphs (TH, HE) and short words reveal further mappings.
Iterate. Each correct guess exposes patterns that make the next guess easier.
How to approach it
Count letters across all three found files together.
Make tentative guesses and apply them, then look at the partly decrypted text for recognisable words.
Refine the mapping until the target file reads as sensible English.
Why it matters
Fixed substitution preserves the statistics of the language. Good modern ciphers are designed so ciphertext looks uniformly random.
docs/wargames/krypton/krypton3/index.htm.title: Krypton Level 3 | Wargames

text: Source: This content is aggregated from overthewire (MIT). Visit the original repository for the latest version.
Level Info
Good job!
You more than likely used some form of FA and some common sense to solve that one.

So far we have worked with simple substitution ciphers. They have also been ‘monoalphabetic’, meaning using a fixed key, and giving a one to one mapping of plaintext (P) to ciphertext (C). Another type of substitution cipher is referred to as ‘polyalphabetic’, where one character of P may map to many, or all, possible ciphertext characters.
An example of a polyalphabetic cipher is called a Vigenère Cipher. It works like this:
If we use the key(K) ‘GOLD’, and P = PROCEED MEETING AS AGREED, then “add” P to K, we get C. When adding, if we exceed 25, then we roll to 0 (modulo 26).
P P R O C E E D M E E T I N G A S A G R E E D\ K G O L D G O L D G O L D G O L D G O L D G O\
becomes:
So, we get a ciphertext of:
VFZFK SOPKS ELTUL VGUCH KR
This level is a Vigenère Cipher. You have intercepted two longer, english language messages (American English). You also have a key piece of information. You know the key length!
For this exercise, the key length is 6. The password to level five is in the usual place, encrypted with the 6 letter key.
Have fun!
Study guide
Level map: logged in as krypton4, decrypt the file that holds the password for krypton5.
What this level teaches
Polyalphabetic ciphers and how knowing the key length turns them back into simple substitution.
Key ideas

Vigenère. A repeating keyword is added letter by letter to the plaintext, modulo 26, so one plaintext letter can encrypt to many different ciphertext letters. The page includes a worked example with the key GOLD.
Defeating the repetition. With a key of length six, every sixth letter was shifted by the same amount. Splitting the text into six groups gives six independent Caesar ciphers.
Frequency analysis per group. Each group is plain shifted English, so the most common letter is likely E (or another common letter) shifted.
Reassemble the key. Once you know the shift for each group, you know the key and can decrypt everything.
How to approach it
Combine the intercepted messages for more data and split them by position modulo the key length.
Count letters in each group and deduce each shift.
Decrypt and read the result; correct any group that gives gibberish.
Why it matters
Vigenère was considered unbreakable for centuries. Once you know how it is attacked, the lesson sticks: repeated keys leak.

text: Source: This content is aggregated from overthewire (MIT). Visit the original repository for the latest version.
Level Info
FA can break a known key length as well. Lets try one last polyalphabetic cipher, but this time the key length is unknown. Note: the text is writen in American English
Enjoy.
Study guide
Level map: logged in as krypton5, decrypt the file that holds the password for krypton6.
What this level teaches
How to find an unknown key length, then reuse the Level 4 method.
Key ideas

Repeated sequences (Kasiski examination). If the same plaintext fragment is encrypted at positions separated by a multiple of the key length, it produces the same ciphertext. Distances between repeats suggest the length.
Index of coincidence. A statistic measuring how uneven the letter distribution is. When you split text by the correct key length, each group looks like English and the statistic jumps.

Look for repeated sequences and note their spacing, or compute the coincidence statistic.
Pick the most plausible key length.
Apply the method from Level 4.

Level Info
Hopefully by now its obvious that encryption using repeating keys is a bad idea. Frequency analysis can destroy repeating/fixed key substitution crypto.

A feature of good crypto is random ciphertext. A good cipher must not reveal any clues about the plaintext. Since natural language plaintext (in this case, English) contains patterns, it is left up to the encryption key or the encryption algorithm to add the ‘randomness’.
Modern ciphers are similar to older plain substitution ciphers, but improve the ‘random’ nature of the key.

An example of an older cipher using a complex, random, large key is a vigniere using a key of the same size of the plaintext. For example, imagine you and your confident have agreed on a key using the book ‘A Tale of Two Cities’ as your key, in 256 byte blocks.
The cipher works as such:

Each plaintext message is broken into 256 byte blocks. For each block of plaintext, a corresponding 256 byte block from the book is used as the key, starting from the first chapter, and progressing. No part of the book is ever re-used as key. The use of a key of the same length as the plaintext, and only using it once is called a “One Time Pad”.

Look in the krypton6 directory. You will find a file called ‘plain1’, a 256 byte block. You will also see a file ‘key1’, the first 256 bytes of ‘A Tale of Two Cities’. The file ‘cipher1’ is the cipher text of plain1. As you can see (and try) it is very difficult to break the cipher without the key knowledge.

If the encryption is truly random letters, and only used once, then it is impossible to break. A truly random “One Time Pad” key cannot be broken. Consider intercepting a ciphertext message of 1000 bytes. One could brute force for the key, but due to the random key nature, you would produce every single valid 1000 letter plaintext as well. Who is to know which is the real plaintext?!?

Choosing keys that are the same size as the plaintext is impractical. Therefore, other methods must be used to obscure ciphertext against frequency analysis in a simple substitution cipher. The impracticality of an ‘infinite’ key means that the randomness, or entropy, of the encryption is introduced via the method.
We have seen the method of ‘substitution’. Even in modern crypto, substitution is a valid technique. Another technique is ‘transposition’, or swapping of bytes.
Modern ciphers break into two types; symmetric and asymmetric.
Symmetric ciphers come in two flavours: block and stream.

Until now, we have been playing with classical ciphers, approximating ‘block’ ciphers. A block cipher is done in fixed size blocks (suprise!). For example, in the previous paragraphs we discussed breaking text and keys into 256 byte blocks, and working on those blocks. Block ciphers use a fixed key to perform substituion and transposition ciphers on each block discretely.

Its time to employ a stream cipher. A stream cipher attempts to create an on-the-fly ‘random’ keystream to encrypt the incoming plaintext one byte at a time. Typically, the ‘random’ key byte is xor’d with the plaintext to produce the ciphertext. If the random keystream can be replicated at the recieving end, then a further xor will produce the plaintext once again.
From this example forward, we will be working with bytes, not ASCII text, so a hex editor/dumper like hexdump is a necessity. Now is the right time to start to learn to use tools like cryptool.

In this example, the keyfile is in your directory, however it is not readable by you. The binary ‘encrypt6’ is also available. It will read the keyfile and encrypt any message you desire, using the key AND a ‘random’ number. You get to perform a ‘known ciphertext’ attack by introducing plaintext of your choice. The challenge here is not simple, but the ‘random’ number generator is weak.
As stated, it is now that we suggest you begin to use public tools, like cryptool, to help in your analysis. You will most likely need a hint to get going. See ‘HINT1’ if you need a kicktstart.
If you have further difficulty, there is a hint in ‘HINT2’.
The password for level 7 (krypton7) is encrypted with ‘encrypt6’.
Good Luck!
Study guide
Level map: logged in as krypton6, decrypt the file that holds the password for krypton7.
What this level teaches
The ideas behind modern cryptography: one-time pads, block and stream ciphers, and what happens when the keystream is not truly random.
Key ideas
One-time pad. A key as long as the message, truly random and never reused, gives perfect secrecy. The page’s example uses a book as a key, which shows why that is not random enough in practice.
Block ciphers vs stream ciphers. Block ciphers work on fixed-size chunks; stream ciphers generate a keystream combined byte by byte, typically by XOR.
XOR. plaintext XOR keystream = ciphertext, and XOR-ing again with the same keystream restores the plaintext.
Weak generator. The program mixes the key with a “random” number that is not strong enough, so the keystream has structure you can exploit.
Work with bytes, not text. Use hexdump or xxd, and tools like CrypTool.
Hints. The level directory contains hint files if you need a push, labelled HINT1 and HINT2.
How to approach it
Read all of the page, including the explanation of keys and streams.
Use the provided encrypt6 program on plaintext you choose, and compare the output carefully across runs.
Look for repetition or predictability in the keystream, and use it on the password file.
Why it matters
Real stream ciphers fail catastrophically when a keystream repeats or is predictable, and many protocols have been broken that way. Never reuse a nonce or write your own cipher.

What this level teaches
How symbolic links (“symlinks”) can trick a privileged program that trusts a predictable path.
Key ideas
Symlinks. A symlink is a small file that points at another path; ln -s TARGET LINKNAME creates one.
