What Manpage teaches
Manpage is about breaking common Linux C-programming misconceptions. Its author’s advice is that a good way to begin auditing code is to read the manual pages for pitfalls and unusual behaviour.
Connecting

Manpage is reached with SSH at manpage.labs.overthewire.org on port 2224. Levels are accounts called manpage0, manpage1 and so on, and the level data is in /manpage/. These games were rescued from the defunct intruded.net with thanks to adc, morla and reth.
Why read the manual?

The author explains that a good tactic when beginning to audit code is to read the manual pages for pitfalls and unusual behaviour, and that many levels were inspired by “the famous work of Ilja”. Typical C pitfalls to look up include:
strncpy does not always NUL-terminate its result.
read and write may transfer fewer bytes than requested.
fgets keeps the trailing newline, and atoi cannot report errors.
snprintf returns the length it wanted to write, not what it wrote.
Mixing signed and unsigned integers in length checks.
access() checks permissions at one moment, and the file may change before it is used.
These are examples of misconceptions to examine, not a list of what the levels contain.
A reconnaissance checklist
ls -l /manpage/ and look at the permissions. A setuid bit marks the program that is your route to the next user.
file and strings on the binary.
Run it normally, then with odd input.
ltrace and strace for library and system calls.
gdb or objdump -d for the logic.
Decide what kind of flaw you are looking at before choosing an attack.
How the levels are numbered
The page for Level N is the account manpageN. Each level’s password is typically stored in a file readable only by the next user, and your task is to get the program for level N to read or reveal it.
Tools
gdb, objdump, ltrace, strace, ghidra, gcc, nc, pwntools, and a notes file for addresses, offsets and observations.
Keep it ethical
Everything here is for the wargame servers. Do not attack other systems, and do not share passwords or complete solutions that would spoil the game for others.

Summary: Difficulty: 2/10 Levels: 10 Platform: Linux/x86 Author: nite Special Thanks: lx_jakal for pointing out a bug that made a level easier =) Description: This wargame is for the ones that want to learn basic exploitation. You can see the most common bugs in this game and we've tried to make them easy to exploit. You'll get the source code of each level to make it easier for you to spot the vuln and abuse it. The difficulty of the game is somewhere between Leviathan and Behemoth, but some of the levels could be quite tricky.
Narnia’s levels are called narnia0, narnia1, … etc. and can be accessed on narnia.labs.overthewire.org through SSH on port 2226.

Study guide
This guide is spoiler-free: it explains what Narnia teaches and how to work, but it never gives finished exploits, payloads or passwords.
What Narnia teaches

Narnia introduces memory corruption: bugs where a program writes outside the space it set aside, letting an attacker change what it does next. The authors rate it 2 out of 10 and place it between Leviathan and Behemoth. You are given the C source code of every level, so the question is never “what does it do?” but “what can I make it do?”.
How the levels are numbered

The page for Level N is the account you are logged in as. You are narniaN and your aim is the password for narniaN+1. Each level’s vulnerable program and source live in /narnia/ (for example /narnia/narnia0 and /narnia/narnia0.c), and the program is setuid to the next user so that exploiting it lets you read that user’s password. The upstream pages deliberately contain no hints.
Concepts you will meet
The stack. Where a function’s local variables and its saved return address are kept. Writing past the end of a local buffer can overwrite things that sit next to it.
Endianness. On x86, multi-byte numbers are stored least-significant byte first, so values you write into memory must be reversed.
Shellcode. Small machine-code programs, usually starting a shell, injected into memory and then run.
Environment variables and arguments. Handy places to put data into a program’s memory.
Format strings. Passing user data as the first argument of printf lets an attacker read and write memory.
Return-to-library. Calling existing library functions instead of injecting new code.
Tools

gdb (with a helper such as pwndbg or gef if you like), objdump, ghidra, gcc, pwntools for scripting exploits, and Python or Perl one-liners for building payloads. The Narnia index suggests exactly these.
A working method
Read the source and ask which function copies or prints user data without checking its size.
Run the program normally and with oversized input to confirm a crash.
Use gdb to find exactly where your input lands and what you overwrite.
Build the smallest payload that proves control, then extend it.
Keep notes on stack layouts you discovered; they differ between levels.
Safety and ethics
Exploit development against your own lab machines and wargames is legal and educational; do not run these techniques against systems you have no permission to test.

What this level teaches
The simplest memory bug: writing more data than a buffer holds so that it spills into the next variable.
Key ideas
Adjacent variables. Local variables sit next to each other on the stack, so overflowing one can change another.
Little-endian values. The target value must be written into memory least-significant byte first.
Printing bytes you cannot type. A printf or perl -e 'print ...' command can emit arbitrary bytes for you.
Keeping the shell open. The program may run a shell that exits immediately if its input ends; read about how to keep standard input open.
How to approach it
Read the source and note the size of the buffer, the other variable and the check that depends on it.
Find the exact number of bytes needed to reach that variable and what value it must hold.
Send the input from a command and keep the connection open so the shell stays usable.
Why it matters
Overwriting an adjacent flag, length or permission field is a real-world pattern as well as a teaching one.

Environment variables are strings the shell passes to every program. Programs can read them and they can be arbitrarily set by the user.

Read the source and note the buffer size and the unsafe copy.
In gdb, crash the program with a pattern to find the offset.

Read the source before debugging. Note every buffer, its size, the variables declared near it and what the program does with them.
Not all overflows target return addresses. Overwriting the right neighbouring variable can be easier and just as powerful.
Files as inputs and outputs. When a program reads and writes files, think about what names you control and what links to other files you could create in a private /tmp directory.
How to approach it
Draw the stack layout of the main function from the source.
Work out which variable your overflow reaches first and how the program uses it.
Test in gdb, then craft the file names or links needed.
Why it matters
Real exploits are usually found by studying program behaviour, not by blindly overwriting return addresses.

Study guide
Level map: logged in as narnia5, find the password for narnia6.
What this level teaches
Format-string vulnerabilities.
Key ideas
Why it happens. Passing a user-controlled string as the format argument lets the user include conversion specifiers such as %x and %n.
Reading memory. %x and positional specifiers like %7$x print values from the stack.
Writing memory. %n stores the number of characters printed so far at an address taken from the stack, so you can control what is written and where.
Address placement. You put the target address in your own input and find its position on the stack.
Reading material. Scut’s format string paper, referenced in the Blacksun reading list, is the classic.
How to approach it
Read the source to see what value must change and how the format string is used.
Print stack values until you find your own input, to learn its position.
Combine padding and %n to write the value you need.
Why it matters
Format-string bugs were once everywhere. Compilers now warn about them, but the technique teaches how arbitrary-write primitives work.

What this level teaches
Reusing existing code rather than injecting your own, a stepping stone to modern exploitation.
Key ideas
Return-to-libc. The C library is already loaded and contains useful functions. Redirecting execution to one with chosen arguments avoids needing shellcode.
Calling conventions. On 32-bit x86, arguments go on the stack; you have to place them where the called function expects.

Read the source closely. The program’s structure determines which pointers or return addresses are reachable.

Read the source and list what can be overwritten and what it controls.
Locate the function you want to call and the string you want to pass it.
Assemble and test the payload in gdb before running it for real.

Return-to-libc leads directly to return-oriented programming (ROP), the standard bypass for non-executable stacks.

Natas
Natas teaches the basics of serverside web-security.

Each level of natas consists of its own website located at http://natasX.natas.labs.overthewire.org, where X is the level number. There is no SSH login. To access a level, enter the username for that level (e.g. natas0 for level 0) and its password.

Each level has access to the password of the next level. Your job is to somehow obtain that next password and level up. All passwords are also stored in /etc/natas_webpass/. E.g. the password for natas5 is stored in the file /etc/natas_webpass/natas5 and only readable by natas4 and natas5.
Start here:
Username: natas0 Password: natas0 URL: http://natas0.natas.labs.overthewire.org
Tools you may find useful to solve this wargame
A webbrowser, curl, ZAP proxy
developed in association with
the NESSoS FP7 project
Study guide
This guide is spoiler-free: it names the concept each level exercises so you know what to study, but it never gives passwords, payloads or finished solutions.
What Natas teaches

Natas is a tour of how web applications fail. There is no SSH login. Each level is its own website at natasN.natas.labs.overthewire.org, protected by HTTP Basic authentication (a browser pop-up asking for a username and password). Your job is to make the site disclose the password for the next level. Along the way you meet most of the classic web vulnerabilities, always from the server side: the flaws are in how the server trusts what the browser sends.
How the levels are numbered

Unlike Bandit, the page for Level N is the level you are in: sign in as natasN and look for the password to natasN+1. Every level’s password is also stored on the server in /etc/natas_webpass/, readable only by that level’s user and the previous one, which is the file the vulnerabilities in later levels aim to read.
The learning path
Levels
Theme
Core ideas
Information disclosure
page source, hidden resources, directory listings, robots.txt
Trusting the client
request headers, cookies, source disclosure, file inclusion
Encodings and weak crypto
reversing an encoding, command injection, XOR
File upload
trusting filenames and file signatures
SQL injection
authentication bypass, blind and time-based extraction
Sessions
predictable IDs, custom session handling, shared state
PHP behaviour
redirects, loose comparison, filters and log files
Deeper flaws
object deserialization, truncation, block-cipher misuse
Perl and PHP internals
injection through language features, uploads, phar
The end (for now)
consolidate and move on
Tools you need
A browser with developer tools. View source, the Network tab (to see requests, headers and cookies) and the cookie viewer cover the first third of the game.
curl. Sends exactly the request you specify, which is how you control headers, cookies and methods. Run curl -u natasN:PASSWORD URL.
An intercepting proxy such as OWASP ZAP or Burp Suite for editing requests in flight.
A scripting language. Python with requests is ideal from the blind-injection levels onward, where you automate hundreds of requests.
How to approach any web level
Use the app as a normal user and note every input: form fields, URL parameters, cookies, headers, uploaded files.
Read all the client-side code and the page source, and follow every link and referenced resource.
When source code is offered, read it as a defender: what does the server assume about each input?
Form a hypothesis, test it with the smallest possible request, and read the response closely.
Staying on the right side of the line
Everything here is meant to be attacked, but only the Natas servers. Never apply these techniques to websites you do not own or have written permission to test.

Study guide
Level map: sign in as natas0 and find the password for natas1.
What this level teaches
That a web page is more than what you see on screen. Your browser receives HTML, CSS and JavaScript, and everything it receives is visible to you.
Key ideas
HTTP Basic authentication. The username and password in the level’s description are sent with every request in a header; the browser pop-up is just a form for that header.
The page source. The browser renders the HTML it was sent but you can read the raw text with “View Source” or the developer tools.
Client-side is public. Anything sent to the browser, including HTML comments, can be read by the user.
How to approach it
Log in with the credentials on this page.
Read the message on the page, then look at what is behind it.
How developers prevent it
Never put secrets, credentials or internal notes in HTML, comments or JavaScript. Treat everything in the response as public.

Study guide
Level map: sign in as natas1 and find the password for natas2.
What this level teaches
A site can try to block “right click” or shortcuts, but cannot stop the browser giving you the data it already received.
Key ideas
Client-side controls are advisory. JavaScript that disables a menu runs on your machine, under your control.
Many ways in. Developer-tools shortcuts, the browser menu, a view-source: URL prefix and curl all bypass the trick.
Think about trust. The server cannot verify anything the browser claims to have done.
How to approach it
Notice what the page says it prevents, and ask which other tools can fetch the same page.
Use a method that never involves the blocked action.
How developers prevent it
Enforce security on the server. Client-side checks are useful for convenience and user experience only, never for access control.

Study guide
Level map: sign in as natas10 and find the password for natas11.
What this level teaches
Why filtering out “bad” characters is fragile, and how to achieve the goal using only characters that are allowed.
Key ideas
Blocklist vs allow-list. A blocklist tries to list everything dangerous and always misses something; an allow-list accepts only what is known to be safe.
Same program, different use. The command being run has options and arguments of its own. Even without chaining, you can steer what it searches and which files it reads.
Read the manual. The program’s man page is as useful here as it was in Bandit.
How to approach it
Compare this level’s code with the previous one and list what changed.
Ask what the allowed characters still let you tell the command to do.
How developers prevent it
Do not construct shell commands from input. Use library functions that search text directly and never hand user data to a shell.

Username: natas11 URL: http://natas11.natas.labs.overthewire.org
Study guide
Level map: sign in as natas11 and find the password for natas12.
What this level teaches
How weak, home-made encryption fails against someone who knows part of the plaintext.
Key ideas
XOR. Combining two byte strings with exclusive-or is reversible: (a XOR b) XOR b = a.
Known-plaintext attack. If you know the original data and see the encrypted result, XOR-ing them together reveals the key.
Repeating key. A short key reused over a long message leaks quickly, as in Krypton’s Vigenère levels.
Forgery. Once you have the key, you can build your own valid cookie.
How to approach it
Read the source to learn what data is stored in the cookie and how it is encoded.
Work out what plaintext the server started with and use it with the cookie value to recover the key.
Create the data you want, encrypt it the same way, and send it back.
How developers prevent it
Never invent encryption. Use authenticated encryption from a trusted library, or keep state on the server and send only a random session ID.

Study guide
Level map: sign in as natas12 and find the password for natas13.
What this level teaches
How an unrestricted file upload can turn into remote code execution.
Key ideas
Uploads become files on the server. If they land in a folder the web server executes, the file can run as a script.
Never trust the client. The filename and extension arrive from the browser, and even hidden form fields can be edited.
Execution depends on extension. The web server decides whether to run or merely serve a file by its name.
What to run. A tiny server-side script that reads the password file is enough.
How to approach it
Upload a harmless file, then find where it is stored and what name it was given.
Inspect the form and the code to see which part of the name the server chooses and which part you do.
Request the uploaded file from the browser to see what happens.
How developers prevent it
Store uploads outside the web root, generate the filename yourself, validate the file’s true type, and serve uploads from a domain that never executes code.

Study guide
Level map: sign in as natas13 and find the password for natas14.
What this level teaches
That validating the first few bytes of a file does not make the whole file safe.
Key ideas
Magic bytes. Image formats start with fixed bytes that identify them. Functions such as PHP’s exif_imagetype look only at those.
Polyglot files. A file can satisfy two formats at once, for example start like an image and contain a script after it.
Same weakness, new gate. The execution risk from the previous level is unchanged; only the filter is different.
How to approach it
Read the new check and work out exactly what it examines.
Build a file that passes that check while still containing your payload.
Use xxd or a hex editor to see your file the way the server does.
How developers prevent it
Re-encode images with an image library (which discards extra content), store them outside the web root, and never rely on a header check alone.

Study guide
Level map: sign in as natas14 and find the password for natas15.
What this level teaches
SQL injection: input that changes the meaning of a database query.
Key ideas
String concatenation is the flaw. The code inserts the username and password directly into a query string, so quotes in your input can end the string and add logic.
Boolean logic. A condition such as 1=1 is always true, so a WHERE clause containing OR of it matches every row.
Comments. SQL comment markers can discard the remainder of a query.
Read the source. The page provides it; the exact query shape tells you what to inject.
How to approach it
Read the query the code builds and imagine the final text for ordinary input.
Work out how to complete or break out of the quoted strings to make the check always succeed.
How developers prevent it
Use parameterised queries (prepared statements) so input is always data, never SQL.

Study guide
Level map: sign in as natas15 and find the password for natas16.
What this level teaches
Extracting data one true/false question at a time when the application never prints query results.
Key ideas
Blind injection. You cannot see data, but you can see whether a condition was true.
Oracle. Each request asks a yes/no question such as “does the password start with this letter?”.
Binary search or character-by-character. With a good strategy, a short script finds a 32-character password in a few hundred requests.
Automation. Write the loop in Python with requests and string.ascii_letters; doing it by hand is impractical.
How to approach it
Confirm the injection works by making the page answer differently for a true and a false condition.
Ask the database about one character at a time using functions such as SUBSTRING or LIKE.
Automate, and print progress as you go.
How developers prevent it
Parameterised queries again, plus rate limiting and monitoring for bursts of near-identical requests.

Level map: sign in as natas16 and find the password for natas17.
What this level teaches
Blind command injection through whatever characters the filter still allows.
Key ideas
Shell expansion. A shell evaluates certain constructs before running the command, so you can influence what runs without using the blocked characters.
Side-channel output. The page still shows whether a word was found, which is the oracle.
Building on earlier levels. The method resembles Level 15, applied to a shell command.
Automation. Guess the secret one character at a time with a script.
How to approach it
Compare this filter with the one from Level 10 and list the characters that are still allowed.
Look up what those allowed characters can still do inside the command you saw.
Use the page’s reply as a true/false signal and automate the guessing.
How developers prevent it
As with all injection bugs: separate data from code. Do not pass user input through a shell at all.

Level map: sign in as natas17 and find the password for natas18.
What this level teaches
Using response time as the only observable signal.
Key ideas
Time as a channel. If the page always looks the same, you can still make the database pause when a condition is true and measure how long the response takes.
Delay functions. SQL dialects provide ways to sleep or run an expensive operation conditionally.
Noise. Network jitter produces false positives, so choose a delay that is clearly larger than normal variation and consider repeating questionable guesses.
How to approach it
Use the previous blind level as your template.
Replace “true/false in the page” with “slow/fast response”.
Time each request in your script and choose a threshold carefully.
How developers prevent it
Use parameterised queries, impose database query time limits, and alert on unusual response times.

Study guide
Level map: sign in as natas18 and find the password for natas19.
What this level teaches
Why session identifiers must be large, random and unpredictable.
Key ideas
Sessions. After login the server gives you an identifier in a cookie, and that identifier alone proves who you are.
Small space. If IDs are just small numbers, an attacker can try them all and eventually find an authenticated admin.
Scripting. Loop over the possible values, set the cookie and look for a change in the response.
How to approach it
Read the source and work out the range of session IDs the application can issue.
Write a loop that sends each candidate in the session cookie.
Detect success by a distinctive difference in the reply.
How developers prevent it
Use long cryptographically random session IDs from your framework, rotate them at login, expire them and bind them to additional checks where appropriate.

What this level teaches
That apparent randomness may hide a predictable structure, which can be decoded and forged.
Key ideas
Decoding the cookie. Compare the cookie values you receive for different usernames and look for a pattern, for example a standard encoding of readable text.
Predictable plus enumerable. Once the format is understood, building candidate values is a short script.
Same goal as before. You are still after the administrator’s session.
How to approach it
Log in with several different usernames and compare the resulting cookie values.
Work out what is being encoded, and what part varies.
Generate candidates for the admin account and test them.
How developers prevent it
Treat session IDs as opaque random tokens. Never derive them from user attributes.

Study guide
Level map: sign in as natas2 and find the password for natas3.
What this level teaches
How to enumerate the resources a page loads and explore the directories they live in.
Key ideas
A page references other files. Images, scripts and stylesheets each have a URL, and those URLs reveal folder names.
Directory listing. If a web server has “autoindex” enabled and a directory has no index page, visiting it lists every file inside.
Walking up the path. Removing the last part of a URL moves you to the parent folder, a basic reconnaissance move.
How to approach it
Read the source and list every resource the page references.
Visit the folder that holds a resource and see what the server shows you.
How developers prevent it
Disable directory listings, keep sensitive files out of the web root, and treat every file reachable by URL as public.

Study guide
Level map: sign in as natas20 and find the password for natas21.
What this level teaches
How custom serialisation formats create injection bugs.
Key ideas
Session storage. Server-side sessions keep a small file or record of values keyed by the session ID.
Line-based format. The handler writes one key value pair per line, so a newline in your input looks like a new entry.
Two requests. The application reads the session at the start of a request, so a poisoned write on one request can take effect on the next.
Read the code. The source for the custom myread and mywrite handlers is the whole puzzle.
How to approach it
Read how a value you supply ends up inside the stored session.
Think about what a line break lets you add.
Make the first request to write the data, and the second to benefit from it.
How developers prevent it
Use your framework’s well-tested session handlers, and encode data (for example JSON) instead of inventing a format that can be broken by delimiters.

Level map: sign in as natas21 and find the password for natas22.
What this level teaches
Trust boundaries between co-located applications, and session sharing across them.
Key ideas
Shared session store. The page mentions a second, “experimenter” site that runs next to this one and can set session data.
Parameter-to-session mapping. The experimenter application copies request parameters into the session without limiting which ones.
Cookie scope. The browser decides when to send a cookie, and you can copy a value from one site’s request to another.
How to approach it
Visit the linked second site and study how it uses your input.
Think about which session value the main site uses to grant access.
Make the second site write that value into a session you then use on the first.
How developers prevent it
Separate session stores for separate trust levels, and never copy arbitrary request parameters into session state.

Study guide
Level map: sign in as natas22 and find the password for natas23.
What this level teaches
How HTTP redirects really work, and how browsers hide what the server sent.
Key ideas
A redirect is a response. The server answers with a status like 302 and a Location header, and may still include a body.
Browsers follow it automatically, so you never see the body of the first response.
curl shows everything. Tools that do not follow redirects, or that print them, reveal the full reply.
Server-side logic does not halt. Code that sets a redirect but does not stop executing still produces output.
How to approach it
Request the page without following redirects and read the whole response.
Study the source to learn which parameter triggers the privileged behaviour.
How developers prevent it
Always stop execution after sending a redirect, and perform the authorisation check before generating any sensitive output.

Level map: sign in as natas23 and find the password for natas24.
What this level teaches
How comparing text and numbers together in a dynamically typed language creates logic holes.

Type juggling. In older PHP, comparing a string with a number converts one into the other, often in surprising ways.

Semtex
Semtex is offline.
Wargame?

This network is a legal environment where you can learn coding/hacking techniques without destroying anything. You have to solve Semtex 0 to get a username/password for login. Once logged in, you have to make your way from one level to the next, each one containing a small security hole/feature that has been installed for you. Your mission is to find out how to exploit the weakness and to cause interesting behavior :)
Rules?

Well you can do anything you want on this box, code, hack, learn, … its all there for gaining knowledge. Please refrain from DOS attacks of any kind, it ruins the fun of you and of others. As long as you behave, everything is possible.
Contribute?
This wargame is from the community for the community. If you want to contribute, send a level plus exploit to aton at packetdropped dot org.
Network programming, reverse engineering, buffer overflows and combinatorial analysis.
Contact : aton at packetdropped dot org
Study guide
This guide describes what each Semtex level asks for, using the upstream level pages, without passwords or complete solutions.
Status

The upstream page states that Semtex is offline. The pages here are therefore best read as a syllabus of ideas you can practise yourself, rather than a game you can currently connect to. Check the upstream Semtex page in case that changes.
What Semtex teaches

The maintainers describe the game as a legal environment in which you solve small security holes or features, each installed for you, and learn coding and hacking techniques without destroying anything. The skills it names are network programming, reverse engineering, buffer overflows and combinatorial analysis. You are asked to refrain from denial-of-service attacks, because they ruin the fun for everyone else.
Connecting (historically)
Level 0 gives you credentials for semtex1, used with SSH on port 2229 at semtex.labs.overthewire.org. Other levels refer to extra hosts and tools such as /semtex/ and /rdx/.
The skills ladder
Levels
Theme
Core skills
Getting started
raw TCP, cleaning a data stream, executable formats
Reversing and tricks
encryption algorithms, function interception, brute force, ptrace
Network games
proxying, multiple source addresses, ICMP and raw sockets
Covert channels and tunnels
restricted shells, big-number maths, timing channels, ICMP tunnels
Protocol weaknesses
weak authentication schemes, process plumbing, race conditions
Skills to bring
C or Python, comfort with sockets (Beej’s guide is linked from Level 0), the ability to read assembly, and willingness to write small tools for each level.
Take-aways

Several levels teach ideas that are very relevant today: covert channels, ICMP tunnelling to bypass firewalls, weak challenge-response schemes and spoofed source addresses. Treat them as study cases, and only experiment on systems you own or are authorised to test.

There is an authentication daemon waiting on brebera port 24012. You connect to it, supply your password and get authenticated. The semtex 12 password will give you user access, the admin password will give you administrator access…

Study guide

What this level teaches
Multi-step network protocols and timing-sensitive attacks.
Key ideas
Two services. You authenticate on one port, then use the other to list and read files, with the privilege level depending on your credentials.
Passwords by level. The Semtex 12 password gives user access, while an admin password gives more.
A fast server. The page asks whether you can be faster, which suggests a timing-dependent weakness.

Random Networking

Make 10 connections to port 24027 from different IP’s. On each connection you will receive a string of 10 ASCII characters. XOR this string with the Semtex5 password, character by character. Then send back the 10 characters followed by another string of exactly 10 characters which identifies you (can be anything within A-Z, a-z, 0-9). The first 10 characters that you send, are different on every connection, the last 10 have to be the same. If you do not send the correct string back within 5 seconds you are disconnected. Once connected with at least 10 different IP’s You will receive the password on one connection, chosen randomly.
**Note: Your connections time out in 2 minutes and you cannot connect from an IP that is still connected. May the sockets be with you. **
Reading Material
Socks5 Request For Comment
Study guide
Level map: the challenge service is on port 24027.
What this level teaches
Working with multiple source addresses and a challenge-response protocol.
Key ideas
Challenge-response. Each connection sends ten ASCII characters that you must combine, character by character, with the Semtex 5 password using XOR, then send back along with your own identifier.
Timing. You have five seconds to answer, and connections time out after two minutes.
Different IPs. You cannot reuse an address that is still connected, so you need several exits, such as proxies.
Reading. The SOCKS5 RFC is linked, as a way of routing connections through other hosts.
How to approach it
Write and test the challenge-response handling on a single connection.
Route ten connections through different addresses, using SOCKS or SSH tunnels.
Keep them open until the password arrives.
Why it matters
It shows how defences based on source IP can be circumvented with proxies.

Non-sniffable data

This level is about some very simple covert channel, about transferring information that cannot possibly be sniffed. There is a socket file in /rdx/nature. It is a local Unix socket. Receive data from it until EOF and save it to a file.
Watch the time between the received bytes. Certain delays mean certain bytes that have been left out (have not been sent).
0-1 s : no special data 1-2 s : 'Q' 2-3 s : 'L' 3-4 s : 'A' 4-5 s : 'V'
you have to take these “unsent” data into your output file too, exactly at the places where they occur.
Thus you are receiving data while not receiving anything.
The output file is a .jpg image :)
Study guide
Level map: read from the Unix socket /rdx/nature until end of file and save the result.
What this level teaches
Covert channels: hiding data in timing so it cannot be sniffed as content.
Key ideas
Timing channel. The delay before each received byte encodes extra data: a pause in the 1–2 second range stands for one letter, 2–3 seconds another, and so on, as the page’s table shows.
Reconstruct the data. Insert the omitted characters exactly where the delays occurred.
The result. The completed file is a JPEG image.
Local Unix socket. A file-like endpoint for local inter-process communication.
How to approach it
Write a reader that records the time between bytes.
Apply the table to insert the hidden bytes.
Verify the output with file and open the picture.
Why it matters
Covert timing channels exist in real malware and in side-channel attacks.

Tunneling your firewall

How do you get data through a firewall that is blocking any tcp connection? You just don’t use a tcp connection, but instead other packets, that might not be filtered. For example network maintenance protocols like ICMP.

There is a raw socket open on a yet unknown host that listens for icmp packets and forwards them to a tcp server that you cannot reach. Your job is to create a client that communicates with this icmp “server”. If everything works, you find yourself in a shell on an unknown system, and can search for the password.
The protocol and the server, that is used by the ICMP tunnel is described in your home directory. If you manage to blackbox analyze it, then you can jump directly from semtex0 to semtex10 :)
You will have to use /rdx/rawwrapper.
Study guide
Level map: use /rdx/rawwrapper to talk to the ICMP “server”; the protocol is described in your home directory.
What this level teaches
Protocol tunnelling over a protocol that firewalls often allow.
Key ideas
Firewalls filter by protocol. If TCP is blocked but ICMP is allowed, data can be wrapped inside ICMP packets.
Raw wrapper. A helper lets you send and receive ICMP from an unprivileged account.
Black-box shortcut. The page says that if you manage to analyse the protocol as a black box, you can jump directly from semtex0 to semtex10.
A shell at the end. A working tunnel lands you in a shell on an unknown system.
How to approach it
Read the protocol document in your home directory.
Build a client that sends and receives framed data inside ICMP.
Use the tunnel to run commands and search for the password.
Why it matters
ICMP and DNS tunnelling are well-known exfiltration techniques, and network monitoring tools look for them.

Vortex
The Vortex wargame is currently composed of 27 levels. Most files you need are in /vortex/. Special thanks to the many people who have helped setup and maintain this wargame.
Many thanks to those who have made sure all levels can be played
Study guide
This guide is spoiler-free: it explains the skills each Vortex level asks for, using only what the level pages say, and never lists passwords or solutions.
What Vortex teaches

Vortex is a long, varied course in low-level security. It begins with a small network programming task, passes through stack overflows, format strings, heap corruption and non-executable stacks, then turns to reverse engineering, weak cryptography and predictable random numbers. Many of its levels run on an old 32-bit x86 machine, so values are little-endian and addresses are 32 bits. The index notes that most files you need are in /vortex/.
Status of the game

The maintainers state the game is composed of 27 levels (0 to 26) and is no longer being expanded. Level 25 is described as lost (kept for history) and Level 26 asks players to create their own level, which is no longer active.
Prerequisites

Finish Bandit, then Narnia and Behemoth. You should be able to read C, use gdb, write simple networked programs and understand the stack. Beej’s guides to C and to network programming, which Level 0 links, are the recommended starting point.
How the levels are numbered

The page for Level N describes the challenge that gives you credentials for the next Vortex account. Some levels are solved over the network and some by logging in to vortex.labs.overthewire.org, as individual pages note.
The skills ladder
Levels
Theme
Core skills
Network programming
sockets, byte order, 32-bit arithmetic
Classic memory bugs
overflows, relocation sections, format strings, archive formats
Brute force and reversing

Level Goal

Your goal is to connect to port 5842 on vortex.labs.overthewire.org and read in 4 unsigned integers in host byte order. Add these integers together and send back the results to get a username and password for vortex1. This information can be used to log in using SSH.
Note: vortex is on an 32bit x86 machine (meaning, a little endian architecture)
Helpful Reading Material
C Programming Introduction
Network Programming Tutorial
Study guide
Level map: connect to port 5842 on vortex.labs.overthewire.org to obtain the credentials for the next account.
What this level teaches
Basic network programming and the realities of 32-bit little-endian data.
Key ideas
Sockets. Create a TCP socket, connect, read and write. The page links Beej’s network programming guide.
Byte order. The server sends four 32-bit unsigned integers in host byte order. The page notes the machine is 32-bit x86, so little-endian.
Fixed-width arithmetic. Think about what a 32-bit unsigned integer can hold and what happens when a sum is too big; the value you send must fit the same format.
Parsing binary data. In Python, the struct module reads and writes binary integers.
How to approach it
Connect with a small script and read exactly the bytes you expect.
Convert them to numbers, add them correctly for the width involved, and send the result in the same format.
Why it matters
Binary protocols and integer width mistakes are the foundation of countless exploits.

The task as stated. The page describes it as finding 100 bits out of a randomly generated, hashed 128-bit key. Read the level’s code to see exactly which bits must match and what you control.

Estimate expected work for the plan you choose.

A Stack Overflow with a Difference

This level is pretty straight forward. Just sit down and understand what the code is doing. Your shellcode will require a setuid(LEVEL4_UID) since bash drops effective privileges. You could alternatively write a quick setuid(geteuid()) wrapper around bash.
NOTE: ctors/dtors might no longer be writable, although this level is compiled with -Wl,-z,norelro. Lookup some information about this e.g. here
Reading Material
Smashing the Stack for Fun and Profit
Bypassing StackGuard and StackShield
Study guide
Level map: logged in as vortex3, obtain access to vortex4.
What this level teaches
Writing shellcode that survives dropped privileges, and understanding binary hardening flags.
Key ideas
Bash drops privilege. The page notes that bash drops effective privileges, so your shellcode needs to call setuid itself, or you can use a tiny wrapper that does setuid(geteuid()).
ctors and dtors. Old writable tables of constructors and destructors were classic overwrite targets.
Relocation hardening. The level is compiled without full relocation read-only (norelro), yet the page notes the tables might no longer be writable; research why.
Reading. “Smashing the Stack” and “Bypassing StackGuard and StackShield” are linked.
How to approach it
Read the code until you can say what it does line by line.
Decide which overwrite target will work on this system, and verify it in gdb.
Write shellcode that sets the right user ID before starting a shell.
Why it matters
Privilege handling in shells and the evolution of mitigations like RELRO explain why old exploit recipes stop working.

MD5 Brute Force
A password is required for the next level. vortex5.c and md5.h. a-z,A-Z,0-9 is the search space. The password length is 5 chars long, it was originally 7 chars long.
Collision(s) tested : 489265082 in 217 second(s), 361 millisec, 101 microsec. Average of 2250932.1 hashes/sec.
Study guide
Level map: logged in as vortex5, obtain access to vortex6.
What this level teaches
How big search spaces are, and how speed (hashes per second) decides what is feasible.
Key ideas
Search space. Letters and digits (a–z, A–Z, 0–9) give 62 choices per position. A five-character password has 62 to the power 5, about 916 million possibilities.

Throughput. The page records a run of roughly 2.25 million hashes per second. At that speed five characters take a few minutes, while the original seven characters (about 3.5 trillion possibilities) would take weeks on that hardware.
Provided source. The code and md5.h are available; you are expected to write or adapt a search.
Optimise. Fast hashing loops in C, multiple cores or GPUs, and early rejection all change the arithmetic.
How to approach it
Read the source to learn exactly what is hashed and what you must match.
Write an efficient search in C, and test it on a small known case first.
Estimate the time before launching the full run.
Why it matters
It explains why password length and slow hashes (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2) matter, and why fast hashes such as MD5 are poor for storing passwords.

Reading Material

Study guide

What this level teaches
How CRC checksums work and why they can be forged.
Key ideas
The requirement. The CRC-32 of the program’s first argument must equal a specific 32-bit value shown on the page.
CRC tables. The program uses a lookup table you may need to extract from the binary.
Linearity. CRCs are linear over a finite field, so you can compute bytes that force any result, which is impossible with a proper cryptographic hash.
Reading. “CRC and How to Reverse It” is linked.
How to approach it
Learn how a table-driven CRC-32 is computed.
Choose how many free bytes you will append or choose and solve for them.

CRCs detect accidental errors, not tampering. Never use them for integrity against an attacker.

Learn Linux and security by playing wargames

Hands-on challenges that teach the command line, web security, cryptography and binary exploitation, one level at a time. Every page comes with a spoiler-free study guide that explains the ideas without giving away the answers.

How it works
Wargames are security challenges played as a game. Each level hides a password; finding it teaches a skill, and the password unlocks the next level.
Play for real
Connect over SSH, or in your browser for Natas, to real, intentionally vulnerable servers run by the OverTheWire community.
Study without spoilers
Every page ends with a study guide: the concepts behind the level, a hint-level approach, and why the skill matters in real work.
Follow a path
Games are grouped by difficulty and ordered so that each one prepares you for the next. Start with the first.
A suggested path
This is the order the OverTheWire maintainers suggest. Skipping ahead is fine, but Bandit's skills are assumed everywhere.
BanditLinux command line and SSH. Do this first.
Natas, Krypton or LeviathanPick one by interest: web, cryptography or reverse engineering.
Narnia, then BehemothBinary exploitation, first with the source code and then without.
Utumno, Maze and beyondHarder binaries, code auditing and mixed advanced topics.

Open any game for its overview, prerequisites and a level-by-level roadmap. The sidebar on every page lists its levels, or browse every level on one page.
